title.en: Why the Cow's Skin Is Loose on the Neck

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 72a 'Why the Cow's Skin is Loose on the Neck', eBook #8299

summary.en: A cow and a carabao flee their cruel master, bathe in a river stripping off their 'clothes,' and in their panic dress in each other's skins — the carabao, being larger, so stretches the cow's garment that her neck-skin hangs loose forever, while his own stays tight.
summary.zh: 牛與水牛逃離狠心主人，褪『衣』下河沐浴；驚慌中錯穿對方之皮——水牛身大，牛衣被撐得頸部永遠鬆垮；水牛自己的皮則愈發緊繃。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. Fansler knows no other variants; cf. the Mindoro cave-god version.

passages.text: There was once a poor farmer who possessed a cow and a carabao, his only wealth; he worked his animals so hard that they often complained, but the cruel master would not even listen to their words. One day the cow, tired of this kind of life, said to the carabao, 'Let us run away from this evil man! Though we are very dirty, he is not willing for us even to take a bath... If we run away from him, however, he will have to do his own work, and then we shall be revenged.' The carabao's spirit was aroused: 'I too have long been meditating escape... We are so ill-treated by our cruel master, that God will have pity on us. Come on! Let us go!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 72 'Why the Cow's Skin is Loose on the Neck'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At a river the cow persuaded the carabao to bathe despite his fear that their master was in pursuit: 'Let us take off our clothes before we go into the water!' They stripped themselves and plunged into the deep, cool river — but less than an hour later they saw their master coming after them with a big stick in his hand. In their haste the carabao put on the cow's clothes and the cow got the carabao's, and as their master was very tired he gave up the chase. Since the carabao was larger than the cow, the skin on the cow's neck has been loose ever since, because the two friends were separated and could never exchange clothes again; and likewise the skin on the carabao's neck has been tight ever since these two animals made their mistake in dressing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 72 'Why the Cow's Skin is Loose on the Neck'; not verbatim.

title.en: The First Loose-Skinned Cow and the First Tight-Skinned Carabao
title.zh: 首頭鬆皮牛與緊皮水牛

region.zh: 菲律賓民都洛島皮納馬拉揚（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog (Mindoro) oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 72b 'The First Loose-Skinned Cow and the First Tight-Skinned Carabao', eBook #8299

summary.en: A cow and carabao sent to scout a mountain cave are seized by the god of the cave, who, fed from their master's provisions, rewards them with dresses of gold and bronze and keeps them as servants. Sent to gather fruit, they bathe in a pond, see their master coming with a big stick, and dress in haste in each other's garments — which become their outer skins: the carabao wears the tight bronze hide, the cow the loose golden one.
summary.zh: 牛與水牛奉命探洞，為洞神所擒；牠們以主人乾糧饗神，神賜金衣、銅衣各一，並留牠們為僕。採果途中戲水，見主人持棍而來，慌亂中互換衣物——自此金銅之衣化為外皮：水牛得緊繃銅色之皮，牛得寬鬆金色之皮。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog (Mindoro) etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Morente narrator; archival record. Cave-god episode; sacred-place tag marks the god's cave on the mountain.

passages.text: Many years ago, when the people of the world were still few in number and the animals took the place of servants, an old man bought a cow and a carabao from his neighbor and travelled with them until he reached the top of a mountain. There they saw a cave, and the old man told his servants to enter and see if there was any danger inside. With slow and cautious steps the carabao and the cow went in, examining every corner; all at once the cow perceived something moving, and in his fright jumped back to hide behind his companion — but the slow-going carabao suddenly felt his hind leg seized in a strong grasp: the god of the cave had caught him. His voice was terrifying, but his words were kind: for many days he had been hungry, and he asked for meat.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 72 'The First Loose-Skinned Cow and the First Tight-Skinned Carabao'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The cow, whose courage had by this time been somewhat restored, gladly offered him some of her master's provisions, which she was carrying; in return for this kindness the god gave each of the animals a dress — to the carabao one of gold, and to the cow one of bronze — and invited the two to remain with him and be his servants. Some time after, the god sent them to gather fruits; they rushed out into the woods, and when they came to a pond took off their new clothes and plunged into the soft mud. While they were enjoying their bath they saw their master coming, carrying a big stick; in their haste to get their clothes back on they made a mistake — the carabao got into the cow's dress, and the cow into the carabao's. After that they never exchanged their clothes, which finally became their outer skin: so to-day the carabao has a tight bronze-colored skin, and the cow a loose golden-colored one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 72 'The First Loose-Skinned Cow and the First Tight-Skinned Carabao'; not verbatim.

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 73 'Why the Monkey is Wise', eBook #8299

summary.en: A pestilence kills six of a poor man's seven sons; the surviving youngest refuses all help to his dying father and runs into the woods. God curses the unfilial son: he loses the power of speech and is condemned to live in the forests ever after as a monkey — and monkeys are wise because they are descended from a human being.
summary.zh: 瘟疫奪走七子中的六人；倖存的小兒子對垂死的父親不聞不問，逃入山林。上帝詛咒這不孝之子：奪其言語，永為林中之猴——猴子雖不能言，卻因源自人類而聰慧。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. One of several Filipino origin-of-monkey myths (see Origin of the Monkey, The First Monkey).

passages.text: Once upon a time there lived a poor man who had seven sons; all except the youngest helped their aged father with the work, but the family became poorer and poorer, and one day, when they had exhausted all their means of support, the father assigned each son a certain kind of work — to the youngest, the task of gathering sticks in the forest for fuel. Not long afterwards a pestilence broke out in the little town where the old man lived, and all his sons but the youngest died.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 73 'Why the Monkey is Wise'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The father was left to starve on his bed, for his only living son was so ungrateful as not to give any help to his father in his last years. When the old man was about to breathe his last, he called his son to give him his final benediction; but the ungrateful boy, instead of going to his dying father, ran away into the woods, and the old man passed away without anybody to care for him. But God punished the unfilial son: he cursed him, and the boy lost his power of speech, and was condemned to live in the forests ever after as a monkey. Thus, although monkeys cannot talk, they are wise because they are descended from a human being.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 73 'Why the Monkey is Wise'; not verbatim.

title.en: Origin of the Monkey: Bathala and the Slipping Mould
title.zh: 猴之起源：巴哈拉的失手

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral creation tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 73, 'Origin of the Monkey', eBook #8299

summary.en: Bathala, lonely in a world divided into earth and heaven, creates rain, gathers clay, and fashions men, birds, plants, mountains, and rivers. While molding a man, the clay slips from his left hand and stretches into a long rope, the mould falling into a tree; in his anger Bathala curses it: 'Thou shalt have life, but thou shalt inhabit trees. The part of thy body that has been stretched out into a rope shall become thy tail' — and the clay became a monkey, great-grandfather of all monkeys.
summary.zh: 巴哈拉因孤寂而造物：降雨取土，捏塑人、鳥、草木、山川。塑人之際，泥坯自左手滑脫，抻成長繩，落入樹中。盛怒的巴哈拉詛咒道：『你有生命，但只能棲樹；被拉成繩的那部分，將成為你的尾巴。』泥坯化作猴子——群猴之太祖。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog creation tale recorded by Fansler from a Maceda narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. Bathala's failed man-mould is a clay-humans variant ending in the first monkey.

passages.text: A long time ago the world, which was divided into earth and heaven, was very lonesome, for Bathala was the only living being in it, and he lived in heaven. One day Bathala felt so lonely that the thought of creating some living beings for his companions came into his mind; he had never thought of this before, although with his infinite power he could do anything he pleased. So he came down to earth to get some clay, but found the ground very dry, for there was no such thing as rain on the earth. Immediately he said, 'Let there be rain!' and the rain fell down. Then, with a large load of slippery clay, Bathala returned to heaven and began the work of creation: he created men, birds, plants, mountains, and rivers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 73, 'Origin of the Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: While he was in the act of creating men, however, an accident occurred. As he was moulding a piece of clay into the shape of a man, the mould slipped from his left hand; Bathala was quick enough to grasp the back of this lifeless mass of clay, but the clay was so soft that it stretched out into a long rope, and the mould fell into a tree. In his anger, Bathala said, 'I curse thee! Thou shalt have life, but thou shalt inhabit trees. The part of thy body that has been stretched out into a rope shall become thy tail.' The lifeless mould was at once changed into a monkey, the great-grandfather of all the monkeys.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 73, 'Origin of the Monkey'; not verbatim.

title.en: The First Monkey: The Weaving Goddess and the Leather Skin
title.zh: 第一隻猴：織神與皮革之皮

region.en: Dingras, Ilocos Norte, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋北伊洛克斯省丁格拉鎮（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Ilocano oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 73, 'The First Monkey' (Ilocano), eBook #8299

summary.en: A girl kept by the goddess of weaving in a happy forest is given cotton to make her own dress, and shrugs off each step of the work — cleaning, beating, spinning, weaving — preferring the leather hide used to beat the cotton, which 'will wear longer.' The goddess decrees that the leather shall become her very skin, thrusts the cotton-beating stick between the maiden's buttocks as a tail, and condemns her to live in trees: thus originated the first monkey with a coat of leather and a tail.
summary.zh: 織神供養的少女在林中無憂無慮，領棉織衣卻嫌洗、捶、紡、織事事麻煩，索性披上捶棉的皮革——『更耐穿』。織神震怒，令皮革成為她的皮膚，將捶棉棒插為其尾，罰其棲樹覓食——第一隻披皮著尾的猴子由此而來。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano etiological tale written down by Sotero Albano (Dingras, Ilocos Norte); archival record. The transformation episode is coarse in the source; paraphrased with restraint. Fansler lists parallel Tinguian and Bagobo lazy-creature-to-monkey myths (Fay-Cooper Cole Nos. 65-67; Benedict).

passages.text: Long years ago there lived in a thick forest a young girl under the care of the goddess of weaving; there she lived happily and without care, for everything that she wanted to eat was provided for her by her patroness. One day the goddess said to the girl, 'Take this cotton, clean it, and make out of it a dress for yourself.' The girl, who knew nothing about making cloth and weaving it, asked whether, once the cotton was cleaned, it was ready for use; the goddess answered that after it was cleaned it must be beaten; after it was beaten, spun; and after it was spun, woven into cloth, cut, and sewed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ilocano tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 73, 'The First Monkey'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Oh!' said the girl, 'it will take a long time and much hard work to make clothes that way. This leather hide, which you have given me to beat the cotton on, will make me better clothing, because it will wear longer.' So she covered herself with the leather. The goddess was so angry at the girl for her laziness that she determined that the leather should not only be her dress but also become her very skin; then the goddess took the stick for beating the cotton and, thrusting it behind the maiden as a tail, said to her, 'This stick will become a part of your body, and you will use it for climbing-purposes. As a penalty for your laziness, henceforth you shall live in trees in the forest, and there you will find your food.' Thus originated the first monkey with a coat of leather and a tail.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Ilocano tale printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 73, 'The First Monkey'; not verbatim. The source's blunt anatomical wording has been moderated; the sense is unchanged.

title.en: The Lost Necklace: Why Hens Scratch and Crows Eat Chicks
title.zh: 失落的項鍊：母雞刨土、烏鴉食雛之由

texts.period: Visayan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 74a 'The Lost Necklace', eBook #8299

summary.en: A crow lends his fine new necklace to the hen, who loses it through her chicks' mischief. Until it is found, the crow exacts one chick a day — so hens and chicks still scratch the ground together searching for the lost necklace, and crows still eat chicks in payment for the lost jewel.
summary.zh: 烏鴉將新買的項鍊借予母雞，項鍊卻被小雞弄丟。烏鴉威脅告官，母雞只好允諾每日賠一隻小雞——至今母雞與小雞仍結伴刨土尋找失落的項鍊，烏鴉仍以食雛抵債。

sensitivity.note: Visayan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Esquivel narrator (story from Cebu); archival record. Companion to The Cock and the Sparrow-Hawk and The Hawk and the Hen.

passages.text: Once a crow bought a fine necklace from a merchant and, very proud of his purchase, put it around his neck so that everybody could see it; then he flew to a beautiful little garden where he met his old friend the hen strutting about with her chicks following her. 'Oh, what a fine necklace you have! May I borrow it? I will return it to you to-morrow without fail,' said the hen, and the crow, who liked the hen, willingly lent her the necklace for a day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 74 'The Lost Necklace'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next morning the hen confessed that the necklace was lost: her chicks had taken it while she was asleep and did not remember where they put it. 'You must pay for it at once, or else I shall go to the king and tell him that you stole my necklace,' said the crow — and the frightened hen had to be satisfied when he added, 'I will take one of your chicks every day in payment of what you owe me. As soon as you find the necklace, give it to me, and then I will stop eating your chicks.' Unto this day hens and chicks can be found together looking for the lost necklace by scratching the ground, and the crows are still exacting payment for the lost jewel by eating chicks; it is said that the hens and chickens will never cease scratching the ground until the lost necklace is found.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 74 'The Lost Necklace'; not verbatim.

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 74b 'The Cock and the Sparrow-Hawk', eBook #8299

summary.en: A young rooster borrows the sparrow-hawk's heirloom bracelet to pass as rich at a fiesta, loses it dancing, and must search until he finds it while the hawk reserves the right to take a chicken from his flock whenever he pleases — hence hawks still carry off young chickens, and cocks and hens scratch the ground crying 'Tac-ta-laoc!' Come and help me.
summary.zh: 年輕公雞借雀鷹的傳家手鐲赴宴裝富，跳舞時失落。雀鷹罰他找到為止，並保留『隨時取走一隻小雞』之權——至今雀鷹仍叼走雛雞，雞群仍刨土找鐲，仰望天空呼叫『快來幫我！』

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Asuncion narrator (Manila); archival record. Third form of the borrowed-jewel punishment cycle.

passages.text: Long ago the sparrow-hawk and the cock were very good friends. Once, when the cocks were going to hold a great fiesta in the neighboring village, a proud young rooster, who wished to get the reputation for being rich and consequently win him a wife, went to the sparrow-hawk and said, 'My friend, please lend me your bracelet! I am going to our fiesta; and I wish to make some young hens there believe that I am rich, in order that they may love me.' The sparrow-hawk answered, 'With much pleasure, my friend.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 74 'The Cock and the Sparrow-Hawk'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The cock went to the fiesta wearing the borrowed bracelet; while he was dancing, however, he lost the jewel and could find it nowhere. 'Since that bracelet was an heirloom, I valued it very highly,' answered the sparrow-hawk. 'You must go back to the place where you think you lost it, and there look for it until you find it. In the meantime I reserve the right to take from your flock a chicken whenever I please.' So, ever since that time, sparrow-hawks are often seen carrying off young chickens, while the cocks have been busy scratching the ground to find the lost bracelet; hens also scratch the soil, for they hate to lose their chicks and want to find the bracelet as soon as possible — they look up into the sky to see if the sparrow-hawk is near; then they scratch the soil vigorously and cry, 'Tac-ta-laoc!' which means, 'Come and help me!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 74 'The Cock and the Sparrow-Hawk'; not verbatim.

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 75 'The Story of our Fingers', eBook #8299

summary.en: In the days of the ancestors all five fingers stood together; hunger struck, and the Thumb proposed stealing. The four virtuous brothers refused — 'we would rather starve and die than steal' — and drove the Thumb out of their community in shame; so the thumb stands separate from the other four, and the little finger, who had nothing to eat, remains lean and weak.
summary.zh: 祖先的時代五指相連。飢餓降臨，拇指提議偷竊；四位正直的兄弟寧願餓死也不偷，羞逐拇指出族。故今日拇指與四指分離；小指因當年無食，至今瘦弱。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. Told as grandfather's answer to a child's question about the thumb.

passages.text: 'Why does our thumb stand separate from the other fingers?' asked little Antonio; and old Julian answered that in the days of long ago the fingers of our ancestors stood together in the same position. One day one of these fingers, the one we call the little finger, became very hungry, and he asked the finger next to him to give him some food. 'O brother! I am hungry also; but where shall we get food?' said the Ring-Finger. 'Heaven is merciful,' put in the Middle-Finger; 'Heaven will give us some.' 'But what if Heaven gives us no food?' protested the Forefinger. 'Well, then,' interposed the Thumb, 'let us steal!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 75 'The Story of our Fingers'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Steal!' echoed the Forefinger. 'Your idea is against morality, against God, against yourself, against everybody. Our conscience will not permit us to steal,' concluded the other three unanimously. 'Oh, no, no! You are greatly mistaken, my friends!' returned Thumb angrily. 'Ay, if that be your plan, you can go your own way,' said the other four fingers. 'As for us, we would rather starve and die than steal.' Then the four virtuous brothers drove Thumb in shame out of their community, and would have nothing more to do with him. 'So that is why we see our thumbs separated from the other four fingers,' concluded old Julian. 'He was a thief; and the other four, who were honest, did not care to live with him. And it is because Little-Finger did not have enough to eat that we see him lean and weak these days.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 75 'The Story of our Fingers'; not verbatim.

region.en: Binalonan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省比納隆安（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pangasinan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 76 'Why Snails climb up Grass', eBook #8299

summary.en: The mud-fish Dalag (head and provider), the dragon-fly (messenger), the wasp (guard), and the snail (cook) share a common house — until Dalag seizes a hook-laden frog and is caught; the vain dragon-fly tightens his neck-tie against a laughing fish until he cuts off his own head; the starving wasp draws in his belt until he breaks in two. Only the snail remains, wandering and weeping, climbing every grass-stalk to look for his friends — as snails still do.
summary.zh: 泥鰍達拉格（家長兼伙伕）、蜻蜓（信使）、黃蜂（衛士）、螺螄（廚子）同居一屋。達拉格抓鉤上之蛙而被捕；虛榮的蜻蜓誤把嘲笑的魚當譏其領帶，越繫越緊直至斷頭；飢餓的黃蜂勒緊『腰帶』直至斷為兩截。只剩螺螄，一路哭泣，攀上每一根草莖張望——至今依然。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Tomeldan narrator (Binalonan); archival record. Explains snails climbing grass-stalks and weeping.

passages.text: Long ago, when the various kinds of animals dwelt together in a kind of community, a dalag (a kind of mud-fish), a dragonfly, a wasp, and a snail agreed to live together in a common house, dividing the household duties according to their power and skill. Dalag, the biggest and strongest, was made the head of the house and to provide food; Dragon-Fly, the swiftest, was made the messenger; Wasp, because of his poisonous sting, was made house-guard and repairer; Snail, too slow for any other duty, was made the cook. Early one day Dalag went out to look for food, saw a big frog swimming helplessly among the duck-weeds, seized it, and started home — but a sharp hook was inside the frog, and poor Dalag was caught fast; a fisherman came, put him in his basket, took him home and ate him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 76 'Why Snails climb up Grass'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Dragon-Fly was sent out to look for him, and before he went he spent a long time arranging his neck-tie; turning his head in all directions, he met Bolasi, a fish whose lips always move in and out on the surface of the water, and became very angry because he thought Bolasi was laughing at his neck-tie. He tightened it; still Bolasi laughed every time he saw him; Dragon-Fly kept drawing his tie tighter and tighter, until at last he cut his own head off, and that was the end of him. Two days later, Wasp and Snail were very hungry — Snail could eat mud, but Wasp could only draw in his belt a little tighter; at last, oppressed by hunger, he flew forth in search of his friends, tightening his belt again and again until he finally broke in two, and that was the end of Wasp.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 76 'Why Snails climb up Grass'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now only Snail was left. He set out from his home and wandered everywhere in search of his three companions, weeping as he went; his food consisted mostly of mud. Whenever he could find a stalk of grass or the stem of a water-plant, Snail would climb up to look around and see if any of his old friends were in sight. Even to-day the snails still weep; and whenever they see a stalk of grass projecting above the surface of the water, they climb up and look around, trying to discover their old friends.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 76 'Why Snails climb up Grass'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Cuttlefish and Squids Produce a Black Liquid

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 77 'Why the Cuttlefish and Squids produce a Black Liquid', eBook #8299

summary.en: Bathala convenes all the fishes in the Dark Sea to appoint officers: the sting-ray sergeant-at-arms, the crocodile cadaver-carrier, the crab a soldier. The late cuttle-fish and squid interrupt, ask for work, are scolded again, and in fury throw mud over all the drawn-up appointments — so Bathala condemns them to carry pouches of mud forever, to move slowly under their heavy loads, and the squid to remain its present size.
summary.zh: 巴哈拉於黑暗之海召集群魚授職：魟為侍衛官（故有其鞭狀尾），鱷為抬棺者（故有其棺形背甲），蟹為士兵（故有其巨螯）。姍姍來遲的墨魚與魷魚屢遭斥責，憤而以泥塗汙所有已繕就之任命狀——巴哈拉震怒，罰其永世身負泥囊、行動遲緩，魷魚更不得再長大。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Ciudadano narrator (Batangas); archival record. Known by both Tagalogs and Visayans, she says.

passages.text: A long time ago, after Bathala had created the fishes, he assigned a certain day for all of them to meet in the Dark Sea, the object of this convention being to appoint some officers. When they reached the assembly hall they found Bathala sitting on a beautiful stone waiting for them; the roll was called, and the cuttle-fish and squid were found absent. After waiting half an hour, Bathala called the meeting to order and appointed the sting-ray sergeant-at-arms (hence all sting-rays now have whip-like tails), the crocodile cadaver-carrier (so now all its children have a coffin-like skin on their backs), and the crab a soldier (so to-day all its descendants have large and strong fore-legs). Bathala had not finished giving out his appointments when the two missing members came, and at once interrupted the meeting by asking what it was all about.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 77 'Why the Cuttlefish and Squids produce a Black Liquid'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Bathala became very angry at the interruption and scolded the cuttle-fish and the squid severely. The rebuke humiliated them so that they agreed between themselves to go get mud and throw it on the official appointments; when they had gotten the mud they came back and asked Bathala to give them something to do, but instead of appointing them to some work he only scolded them for being late. Angered, they now threw mud on all the appointments that had already been drawn up. This insulting act so enraged Bathala that he stood up and said in thundering tones, 'Now I shall punish you. From this time on, you and your descendants shall carry pouches of mud with you all the time. Besides, you shall be very slow in moving because of your heavy loads.' The squid tried to make excuses, but Bathala became angrier than ever: 'You are the naughtiest creature I ever had. As a punishment, you and your children shall remain the same size as you are now.' And all of Bathala's words have turned out to be true.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 77 'Why the Cuttlefish and Squids produce a Black Liquid'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why Cocks Have Combs on Their Heads

region.zh: 菲律賓馬林杜克島博阿克（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 78 'Why Cocks have Combs on their Heads', eBook #8299

summary.en: The magician Pablo finds his idle son Juan combing his hair before a mirror instead of working; he snatches the comb, strikes the boy's head so hard the comb sticks deep into the skull, and curses, 'Since you always want to use the comb, let it be on your head forever!' — transforming Juan into a cock, the comb into flesh, visible to this day on the heads of all his descendants.
summary.zh: 魔術師帕布洛撞見懶兒胡安對鏡梳頭而不做事；他奪梳怒擊其首，梳齒深陷顱骨，並咒曰：『你既愛梳，就永遠梳在頭上吧！』胡安化為公雞，梳齒化為肉冠——今之雄雞頂冠皆是胡安之後裔。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Nieva narrator (Boac, Marinduque); archival record.

passages.text: Once upon a time there was a magician named Pablo, who had a son called Juan. Pablo was very industrious, but Juan was lazy and disobedient: he cared for nothing but fine clothes and his own appearance, and would not help his father. One day Pablo went into his son's room to find out what he was doing; there he was, standing before a mirror and combing his hair.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 78 'Why Cocks have Combs on their Heads'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Pablo was so angry at his son that he immediately snatched the comb from his hand; then he angrily struck the boy's head with the comb, and spoke these harsh words: 'Since you always want to use the comb, let it be on your head forever! I prefer to have no son at all. I would rather see you changed into a bird than to remain such a disobedient, worthless boy.' The father struck his son's head so hard that the comb stuck deep into the skull; by Pablo's magic power, Juan was immediately changed into a cock, and the comb on his head was changed into flesh. We can see it to-day on the heads of all the descendants of Juan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 78 'Why Cocks have Combs on their Heads'; not verbatim.

title.en: How the Crow Became Black: Bathala's Inkstand
title.zh: 烏鴉變黑：巴哈拉的墨水瓶

region.en: Cagayan de Oro, Misamis, Mindanao, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓民答那峨米薩米斯卡加延德奧羅（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Visayan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79a 'How the Crow became Black', eBook #8299

summary.en: When Bathala's subjects steal Dumagat's fish, the sea-god opens the great pipe of the world's waters and floods the land, drowning nearly all the people. Bathala sends the crow, his pretty-plumaged favorite, to learn whether his subjects survived; the crow lands on the floating corpses and eats. The dove sent after him reports his disobedience, and Bathala seizes his big inkstand and hurls it — the crow covered black forever, condemned to be a scavenger hated by all, while the faithful dove becomes the beloved pet.
summary.zh: 巴哈拉子民偷食海神杜馬加特之魚；海神開啟世水巨管，洪水沒陸，生民幾絕。巴哈拉遣羽色絢麗的寵鳥烏鴉探查；烏鴉卻落於浮屍啄食。奉命尋找的鴿子告發其悖命；巴哈拉怒擲墨水瓶——烏鴉被潑成永黑，貶為人人憎惡的食腐者；忠實的鴿子則成眾人所愛。

sensitivity.note: Visayan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Neri narrator (Cagayan, Misamis); archival record. Flood cluster: the deluge here issues from a quarrel between two pagan deities, which Fansler reads as preserved old native tradition.

passages.text: A long time ago, when Bathala, the god of the land, was peacefully ruling his dominions, he had many pets, and among these his two favorites were the dove and the crow; the crow was noted for its bright, pretty plumage. One day Bathala had a quarrel with Dumagat, the god of the sea: Bathala's subjects had been stealing fish, which were the subjects of Dumagat. When Dumagat learned of this, and could get no satisfaction from Bathala, he retaliated: he opened the big pipe through which the water of the world passes, and flooded the dominions of Bathala, until nearly all the people were drowned.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'How the Crow became Black'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the water had abated somewhat, Bathala sent the crow, his favorite messenger, to find out whether all his subjects had been killed. The crow flew out and soon saw the corpses of many persons floating about; he descended, alighted on one, and began to eat the decaying cadaver. When Bathala saw that it was late and the crow had not returned, he sent the dove on the same errand; the dove, looking for any signs of life, at last saw the crow eating the decaying bodies, told him the king had sent for him, and together they flew back to Bathala's palace, where the dove reported that the crow had been eating dead bodies and had not done what he was sent to do.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'How the Crow became Black'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Bathala was very angry at this disobedience. Without saying a word, he seized his big inkstand filled with black ink and threw it at the crow, which was immediately covered. Then he turned to the dove: 'You, my dove, because of your faithfulness, shall be my favorite pet, and no longer shall you be a messenger.' And to the crow: 'You, foul bird, shall forever remain black; you shall forever be a scavenger, and every one shall hate you.' So that is why to-day the dove is loved by the people and the crow hated; the crows to-day are all black, because they are descendants of the bird punished by Bathala.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'How the Crow became Black'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Crow Is Black: The Crows of Sinukuan
title.zh: 烏鴉變黑：蘇努庫安的雙鴉

region.en: Tarlac province, Luzon, Philippines (Pampangan tale, Ilocano narrator's home)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋丹轆省（邦板牙故事，伊洛卡諾敘述者居地）

texts.period: Pampangan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79b 'Why the Crow is Black', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two golden-plumaged crows sing in the gardens of Sinukuan's palace while a pestilence kills his animals. Returning from three days of relief among his dying subjects, he calls for his birds to sing away his anguish — and finds them feasting on decaying carcasses a mile away. Restraining himself from killing them, he curses them to be ugly black birds with only a harsh cry: the crows of today.
summary.zh: 瘟疫肆虐，蘇努庫安的金羽雙鴉卻在金園中歌唱。神行三日救疫歸來，喚鴉歌以解憂——竟見牠們在屍堆中饗腐肉。祂強忍殺意，咒其化為醜黑之鳥、聲啞而厲——今日之烏鴉即其後裔。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Ortega narrator (an Ilocano living in Tarlac); archival record. Sinukuan is the great Pampangan mountain-deity; no flood in this version, the occasion being a pestilence.

passages.text: The first crow that lived on the earth was a beautiful bird with a sweet voice. The universe was ruled over by the god Sinukuan, and all his subjects were either plants or animals, no human beings yet being in existence. Sinukuan lived in a beautiful palace surrounded with gardens of gold, and in these gardens lived two crows who sang sweet songs and did nothing but fly about among the flowers and trees; their golden plumage was beautiful to see, and Sinukuan took great delight in them. Once a terrible pestilence visited the earth, and a great many of Sinukuan's animals began to die.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'Why the Crow is Black'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In his distress and sorrow Sinukuan at once set out and made a tour of his kingdom to give what relief he could to his suffering subjects; after being away three days he returned to his palace, his mind weighted down by all the death and sickness he had seen, and called to his two birds to come sing for him and relieve his mental anguish — but neither of the birds came. He went through his gardens and called in vain; thinking they had flown away and been attacked by the pestilence, he made another trip through his kingdom to look for them. He had not walked a mile when, approaching a number of dead animals, he saw the pair feasting on the decaying flesh; when they saw their master, they bowed their heads in shame.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'Why the Crow is Black'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Had not Sinukuan restrained himself, he might have killed them that very moment; but he thought of a better way to punish them. 'Now,' he said, as he cursed them, 'from this time on, you shall be very ugly black birds; you shall lose your beautiful voice, and shall be able to make only a harsh cry.' From that time on those birds were black, and their offspring are the crows of to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'Why the Crow is Black'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dove and the Crow (Zambal): The Flood's Red Water

region.en: Cabangan, Zambales, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋三描禮士省卡邦安（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Zambal oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79c 'The Dove and the Crow', eBook #8299

summary.en: After the inundation of the world, God sends a crow to measure the water; finding dead animals everywhere, he forgets his command and stays to eat. The faithful dove, sent three days later, stands in the water reddened by the blood of the slain, finds it only an inch deep, and returns with crimson feet as evidence. The crow, returning without excuse, is punished with a chain on his legs — so crows can only hop from place to place, while the dove remains God's favorite with red feet to this day.
summary.zh: 洪水之後，上帝遣鴉探水深；鴉見遍地死獸，忘命飽食。三日後遣鴿——忠實的鴿子立於血染之水，量得水深僅一吋，紅足為證而歸。無辭以對的鴉被罰以鎖鏈繫足——至今只能跳不能走；忠鴿則為上帝至愛，紅足猶存。

sensitivity.note: Zambal etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Carpio narrator (Cabangan); archival record. Flood-cluster variant: the raven-and-dove post-diluvian measuring episode in Philippine dress; Fansler traces the ultimate source to Arabian tradition (Tabari) via the Moros, noting uniquely Philippine details (the deity, the chained legs).

passages.text: A few days after the inundation of the world, God sent a crow down to earth to see how deep the water was on the land. When the crow flew down to earth, he was surprised to see so many dead animals everywhere; it came to his mind that perhaps they would taste good, so he alighted on one of them and began to eat. He was so very much pleased with the abundance of food about him that he forgot all about the command God had given him, and he remained on the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'The Dove and the Crow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the third day, since the crow had not returned, God sent a dove down to earth to find out the depth of the water and to make other observations of the things that had taken place on the earth. As the dove was a faithful creature, she did not forget what God told her: she did not alight on any dead animal, but alighted directly in the water — now red from the blood of so many creatures that had been slain — and found that it was only an inch deep. She at once flew back to heaven, where, in the presence of God, she related what she had seen on earth, while the crimson color on her feet was evidence of the depth of the water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'The Dove and the Crow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: After a short time the crow returned, and came before God, who spoke to him thus: 'What made you so long? Why did you not return sooner from the earth?' As the crow had no good reason to give for his delay, he said nothing; he simply bent his head. God punished the crow by putting a chain on his legs — so that to-day the crow cannot walk: all he can do is to hop from place to place. The dove, which was faithful to God, is now the favorite pet bird the world over, and the red color on her feet may be seen to-day as evidence that she performed her duty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 79 'The Dove and the Crow'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Ocean Is Salty: Ang-ngalo's Salt Bricks
title.zh: 海為何是鹹的：安恩加洛的鹽磚

region.en: Bangued, Ilocos Sur, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋南伊洛克斯省邦基（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Ilocano oral etiological myth; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 80 'Why the Ocean is Salty', eBook #8299

summary.en: Ang-ngalo, only son of the god of building and Adam of the Ilocanos, digs caves in the mountains and wades the ocean — whose deep caverns are his footprints — to reach Sipnget, goddess of the dark, who demands a mansion of bricks as white as snow. Only salt is white enough; Asin, ruler of the kingdom of Salt, supplies pure salt bricks, and millions of men carry them across hundreds of bamboo bridges until Ocean, her slumber disturbed, sends big waves that bury bridge, carriers, and burden in her deep bosom — and in time the salt dissolved, and today the ocean is salty.
summary.zh: 建築神之獨子、伊洛卡諾人之亞當——巨人安恩加洛，鑿山為洞，蹚海赴約——海底深穴即其足跡。黑暗女神希普內特求建『白如雪之磚』的宮殿；世上唯鹽最白，鹽國之主阿辛獻純鹽磚。百萬人晝夜經竹橋運磚，直至海洋女神不堪其擾，掀起巨浪將橋樑、運夫與磚石盡沒其懷——鹽既溶，海水至今是鹹的。

sensitivity.note: Ilocano etiological myth recorded by Fansler from a Paredes narrator (Bangued); archival record. Ang-ngalo (Aolo) is the giant Adam of the Ilocanos per Blumentritt; the primordial ocean is 'the accumulated tears of disappointed goddesses.'

passages.text: A few years after the creation of the world there lived a tall giant by the name of Ang-ngalo, the only son of the god of building. Ang-ngalo was a wanderer and a lover of work; he lived in the mountains, where he dug many caves, protecting them from the continual anger of Angin, the goddess of the wind, by precipices and sturdy trees. One bright morning, while Ang-ngalo was climbing to his loftiest cave, he spied across the ocean — the ocean at the time was pure, its water being the accumulated tears of disappointed goddesses — a beautiful maid, who beckoned to him and waved her black handkerchief; so Ang-ngalo waded across to her through the water, and the deep caverns in the ocean are his footprints.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 80 'Why the Ocean is Salty'; not verbatim.

passages.text: This beautiful maid was Sipnget, the goddess of the dark. 'I am tired of my dark palace in heaven. You are a great builder. What I want you to do for me is to erect a great mansion on this spot. This mansion must be built of bricks as white as snow.' Ang-ngalo could not find any bricks as white as snow — the only white thing there was then was salt; so he went for help to Asin, the ruler of the kingdom of Salt, who gave him pure bricks of salt as white as snow. Then Ang-ngalo built hundreds of bamboo bridges across the ocean, and millions of men were employed day and night transporting the white bricks from one side of the ocean to the other.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 80 'Why the Ocean is Salty'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At last the patience of Ocean came to an end: she could not bear to have her deep and quiet slumber disturbed. One day, while the men were busy carrying the salt bricks across the bridges, she sent forth big waves and destroyed them; the brick-carriers and their burden were buried in her deep bosom. In time the salt dissolved, and today the ocean is salty.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 80 'Why the Ocean is Salty'; not verbatim.

region.en: Santo Tomas, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省聖托馬斯（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81a 'Why the Sky is Curved', eBook #8299

summary.en: When souls went directly to heaven, heaven grew crowded until the sky began to fall on God's throne; he summoned five angels to hold up the sky with their heads while his carpenters repaired the heavens — and because the tallest angel stood in the centre of the group, the sky has been curved ever since.
summary.zh: 人死即昇天的年代，天堂人滿為患，天穹壓向神座。上帝召五天使以頭頂天，命木匠搶修天宮——因最高者立於中央，天穹從此呈弧形。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Malvar narrator (Santo Tomas, Batangas); archival record. Fansler knows no variants.

passages.text: Many, many years ago, when people were innocent, as soon as they died, their souls went directly to heaven. In a short time heaven was crowded with souls, because nearly every one went there. One day, while God was sitting on his throne, he felt it moved by some one; on looking up, he saw that the souls were pushing towards him, because the sky was about to fall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81 'Why the Sky is Curved'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At once he summoned five angels, and said to them, 'Go at once to the earth, and hold up the sky with your heads until I can have it repaired.' Then God called together all his carpenters and said, 'Repair the heavens as soon as possible.' The work was done; but it happened that the tallest angel was standing in the centre of the group — and so, ever since, the sky has been curved.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81 'Why the Sky is Curved'; not verbatim.

region.en: Janiuay, Iloilo, central Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓怡朗省哈紐艾（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Visayan oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81b 'Why the Sky is High', eBook #8299

summary.en: In olden days the sky was low enough to touch with a stick, so God could hear his people and send blessings — until a drunken sayao dancer at chief Abing's feast darted his spear and pierced the sky, wounding one of the gods; the angered Father raised the sky far from the earth as we have it today.
summary.zh: 昔天天低，竹竿可及——神諦聽民呼、隨時降福。酋長阿賓設宴，酒醉的戰舞者擲矛刺破天穹、傷及神明；盛怒的天父將天升高至今日的遙遠之處。

sensitivity.note: Visayan etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Lutero narrator (Janiuay, Iloilo); archival record. A Malayan tradition: Fansler parallels the Bagobo 'Why the Sky Went Up' myths (Benedict) and Borneo versions (Hose-McDougall; Evans' Horned Owl and the Moon), plus Mabel Cook Cole's Bukidnon pestle-and-sky tale already in the corpus.

passages.text: In olden days the sky was low — so low that it could be reached by a stick of ordinary length. The people in those days said that God had created the sky in such a way that he could hear his people when they called to him, and in turn God could send his blessings to earth as soon as men needed them. Because of this close connection between God and his subjects, the people were well-provided for and did not need to work: whenever they wanted to eat, they would simply call God, and almost before their request was made the food would be on the table. But after the expulsion of Adam and Eve, God made men work for their own living; and with this change in their condition came the custom of holding feasts, when the men would rest from their labors.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81 'Why the Sky is High'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day one of the chiefs, Abing by name, held a feast, and many people came to enjoy it. A sayao, or native war-dance, was given in honor of the men belonging to the chief, acted by men brandishing spears. While acting, one of the dancers, who was drunk, tried to show his skill, but he forgot that the sky was so low: when he darted his spear, he happened to pierce the sky, and one of the gods was wounded. This angered God the Father: so he raised the sky as we have it to-day, far from the earth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 81 'Why the Sky is High'; not verbatim.

title.en: An Unequal Match: Why the Carabao's Hoof Is Split
title.zh: 不對等的較量：水牛蹄為何開裂

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 82 'An Unequal Match; or, Why the Carabao's Hoof is split', eBook #8299

summary.en: Mocked as a slow thing unfit to hunt with him, the turtle challenges the carabao to a seven-hill race under threat of being called a coward; he stations a turtle-friend atop each hill, so the carabao finds his rival always ahead crying 'Here I am!' Convinced of defeat at the seventh hill, the carabao kicks the turtle — whose shell is unharmed, but whose hoof-splitting blow the carabao's own hoof bears to this day.
summary.zh: 水牛譏龜遲緩、不配同行；龜以『懦夫』相激，訂下七丘之賽——每丘頂伏一龜友，水牛每到一丘，總見對手在前大喊『我在這裡！』。第七丘認輸的憤怒水牛一腳踢去——龜殼無恙，龜蹄卻從此開裂。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Rivera narrator (Pagsanjan); archival record. The trickster-race cycle; Fansler parallels the Pampangan 'Deer and Snail' (deer's gall sucked out, snails bitter) and Visayan and Tinguian variants, and the Borneo plandok-and-crab race.

passages.text: Once a carabao and a turtle met on a road and walked in the woods, having a fine talk together. The turtle was a sort of humorist, constantly giving exhibitions of his dexterity in getting food by trickery; but he was especially anxious to win the friendship of the carabao, thinking that the big fellow would help him whenever he got into trouble. 'Let us live together and hunt out food together! thus we shall break the monotony of our solitary lives.' But the carabao snorted: 'You slow thing! you ought to live with the drones, not with a swift and powerful person like me.' Offended, the turtle challenged the carabao to a race; and when the carabao refused, thinking it a disgrace to run against a turtle, the turtle threatened to go to all the forests, woods, and mountains and tell all his friends and the whole animal kingdom that the carabao was a coward.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 82 'An Unequal Match'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now the carabao was persuaded, and asked three days to get ready; the agreement was that the race should extend over seven hills. The turtle at once set out to visit seven of his friends, and by telling them that winning would be to the glory of the turtle kingdom got them to help — so the next day he stationed a turtle on the top of each hill, after giving them all instructions. On the third day the race began, and when the carabao reached the second hill he was astonished to see the turtle ahead of him shouting, 'Here I am!' — the turtle at once disappearing; and at every hill the carabao found his enemy ahead of him. When the carabao was convinced at the seventh hill that he had been defeated, he became so angry that he kicked the turtle; on account of the hardness of its shell the turtle was uninjured, but the hoof of the carabao was split in two because of the force of the blow. And even to-day the carabaos still bear the mark which an unjust action on the part of their ancestor against one whom he knew was far inferior to him in strength produced on himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 82 'An Unequal Match'; not verbatim.
